name: Kranzberg's First Law
statement: Technology is neither good nor bad; nor is it neutral.
meaning: A technology's effects are not fixed by the device itself — they depend on the context, scale, and circumstances of its use. It is 'not neutral' because deploying it is never a consequence-free act: the same tool can be a boon in one setting and a threat in another.
mechanism: Technology does not act in a vacuum; it interacts with what Kranzberg called the 'social ecology'. Because outcomes emerge from that interaction rather than from the artefact alone, identical technologies produce divergent results across different social, economic, and ecological contexts — and the effect can even reverse from beneficial to harmful once a benign technology is used at massive scale.

examples.text: Kranzberg's headline case: DDT raised farm yields and killed disease-carrying pests — then was found to threaten whole ecological systems, from birds and fish up the food chain. The same technology, its verdict reversed once used at scale.

The same passage shows context-dependence directly: wealthy nations banned DDT because they could afford alternatives, while India kept using it because it was cheaper and, crucially, central to preventing malaria. Good or bad depended on the setting, not the chemical.

variants.name: The other five laws
variants.text: The first of six. The rest: invention is the mother of necessity; technology comes in packages, big and small; non-technical factors take precedence in technology-policy decisions; all history is relevant, but the history of technology is the most relevant; and technology is a very human activity.

whyItMatters: It is the founding corrective of technology studies, cutting between two lazy extremes: the techno-optimist who thinks a tool is simply good, and the determinist who thinks its effects are inevitable. It insists that consequences are made in context — which is why the same invention demands different judgements in different places and times.

working.lead: Judge a technology in context, not in the abstract
working.text: ask not 'is this good or bad?' but 'good or bad for whom, at what scale, in which setting?' — the answer changes with all three.
many harms appear only when a benign technology is used massively; weigh the widespread deployment, not just the pilot.
'it's just a tool' is the move the law forbids — deploying a technology reshapes its surroundings and picks winners and losers whether or not anyone intended it to.

limits: Kranzberg himself called his laws 'truisms, not commandments' — interpretive aphorisms from a lifetime studying technology, not scientific laws. The first is nearly unfalsifiable by design: any outcome can be read as confirming that technology is 'not neutral'. 'Neutral' is loosely defined, the law offers orientation rather than prediction, and it can be invoked to excuse almost any technology's harms as merely 'context-dependent'. Its strength is as a framing that resists both utopian and determinist thinking, not as a testable proposition.
misreadings: It is not a claim that technology is bad, nor a shrug that its effects are random. 'Neither good nor bad, nor neutral' means the value is realised in use and context — so the same technology can help and harm, and 'it's just a neutral tool' is precisely the evasion the law rejects.
origin: Stated by the historian Melvin Kranzberg as the first of six laws in his 1985 presidential address to the Society for the History of Technology, published as 'Technology and History: Kranzberg's Laws' in Technology and Culture, 27(3), 1986. Kranzberg was a founder of the society and long-time editor of its journal.

sources.text: Kranzberg, M. (1986). "Technology and History: 'Kranzberg's Laws.'" Technology and Culture, 27(3), 544–560. — the six laws and the DDT example, verbatim.
Melvin Kranzberg, Wikipedia. — biography, the six laws, and his role in founding the history of technology as a field.
